# TICKET-2 (#4163) — revocation callbacks never arrive

Nothing in `reference/` changed since the notes above. This section pulls together what bears on
TICKET-2: first the reference facts, then what the code does. The code facts are separate so you
can tell which source each claim comes from. Where something is my inference, it says so.

## T2.1 From `reference/`

- **Hard 10 s limit.** One invocation handles one status-change event (`batch_size: 1`). The
  invocation is killed at `timeout_seconds: 10`, and "work still in progress at that point is
  abandoned". — `infra/webhook-config.yaml:10-14, 20-22`
- **Nothing retries or catches an abandoned event.** `maximum_retry_attempts: 0` and
  `on_failure_destination: none`. — `infra/webhook-config.yaml:24-27`
- **Outbound timeout covers the connect only.** `outbound_connect_timeout_ms: 2000` is the only
  timeout configured for outbound traffic. The config says nothing about a response or read
  timeout. *(Inference: an endpoint that accepts the connection and never answers is not cut
  off by this setting.)* — `infra/webhook-config.yaml:29-31`
- **`tenant-settings` table.**
  - The partition key is `tenant`, the issuer DID. — `infra/webhook-config.yaml:35`
  - A Query returns 100 items per page. — `:38`
  - A GSI, `tenant-kind-index` (partition `tenant`, sort `kind`, projection `all`), exists for
    looking up one kind of setting directly. — `:39-43`
- **No alarms are configured** (`alarms: []`). Logs go to `/platform/status-notifier` at level
  `info`, with 14-day retention. — `infra/webhook-config.yaml:46-53`
- **Probes must not target reserved domains.** A probe or health-check target must be "an
  endpoint the platform operates, reached over the same path as the traffic it vouches for".
  Reserved names must not be the target of "any check whose result is reported as the state of
  a platform service". A response from `example.com` "says nothing about the state of any
  platform service". — `infra/reserved-domains.md:8-11, 24-26, 33`
- **Linting only covers `deploy.yaml`.** It rejects reserved names in `deploy.yaml` files only.
  A URL constant in service code is not linted. — `infra/reserved-domains.md:38`

## T2.2 From the code

- **Order of work in `Notifier::notify`** (`backend/src/notifier.rs:136-155`):
  1. POST to each platform subscriber. The canary is first (`:118`, `:141-146`).
  2. Read the tenant's full subscription list (`:147`).
  3. POST to each subscriber, one at a time, awaiting each call (`:147-149`).
  4. The whole sequence runs inside `tokio::time::timeout(DISPATCH_BUDGET)`, where
     `DISPATCH_BUDGET` = 10 s (`:23`, `:152`).
- **How subscriptions are read.** `subscriptions()` pages through the tenant's **whole** settings
  partition with `query()` (`notifier.rs:158-169`). Each page costs `PAGE_READ_LATENCY` = 50 ms
  and holds up to `PAGE_SIZE` = 100 items (`settings.rs:17, 20, 80-81`). It never uses
  `query_kind()`, the lookup through the `tenant-kind` index (`settings.rs:100-113`).
- **No per-call timeout.** `dispatch()` awaits `transport.post` with nothing around it
  (`notifier.rs:172-181`). `Endpoint::Hang` never resolves (`webhook.rs:120`).
- **When the budget runs out**, the remaining work is dropped. Only an `eprintln!` is written
  (`notifier.rs:152-154`). Subscribers that were never attempted get no `DeliveryEvent`.
- **What the health check reads.** `canary_healthy()` returns `canary_ok`
  (`notifier.rs:130-132`). `canary_ok` is set only from the canary's own POST result
  (`:143-145`), and that POST happens before the tenant's subscriptions are read.
- **Where the canary points.**
  - In production it is `CANARY_URL` = `https://example.com/webhooks/status`
    (`notifier.rs:29`).
  - In tests, `HermeticTransport::new()` routes that host to an instant 200
    (`webhook.rs:84-87`).
- **What the existing tests cover.** `tests/notifier.rs` uses only "small" tenants: 12
  preferences and 3 subscribers, every endpoint `ok()` or `503`
  (`tests/notifier.rs:26-40, 116-127`).

## T2.3 Measured, with `tokio` time paused (scratch run, not in the repo)

| Settings in partition | Subscribers | Delivered | `canary_healthy()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15,000 | 3 | 3/3 | true |
| 19,500 | 3 | 1/3 | true |
| 20,000 / 50,000 | 3 | 0/3 | true |
| 0 | 66 | 66/66 | true |
| 0 | 67 / 100 | 66/67, 66/100 | true |

From the constants, the budget covers about 200 page reads (10 s / 50 ms), or about 66
deliveries (10 s / 150 ms).

## T2.4 Open questions for TICKET-2

- How many settings the league actually has, and how many relying parties subscribe to it.
- Whether production logs under `/platform/status-notifier` show the `did not finish within`
  line. *(Inference: the runtime limit and `DISPATCH_BUDGET` are both 10 s, and the runtime's
  clock starts first, so the runtime probably kills the invocation before the line is written.)*
- What `example.com` actually returns to the canary's POST in production. The ticket says the
  health check is green, which suggests a 2xx. That can't be checked from here.

# Research notes — `reference/`

Everything I found in `reference/`, with a citation for each point. These notes only say what the
reference documents say. I compared them against our code in a separate reply; that comparison
isn't in this file. The "Open questions" section at the end lists things these documents don't
answer.

## 0. What `reference/` is

- It's a vendor snapshot of external specs, service contracts and infra config. The owning teams
  keep the originals, and this copy is synced from them. — `reference/README.md:3-6`
- It's read-only. Local edits get overwritten on the next sync. — `reference/README.md:8`
- The contents table lists six items: `did-web-method.md`, `trust-registry.md`,
  `infra/did-hosting.md`, `infra/hosted-dids/`, `infra/webhook-config.yaml` and
  `infra/reserved-domains.md`. — `reference/README.md:12-19`

## 1. `did:web` method (`reference/did-web-method.md`)

- It's based on the W3C CCG did:web spec and DID Core 1.0, "as implemented by the platform". — `:3-4`
- A DID must start with `did:web:`. — §1, `:8`
- The identifier is a domain plus an optional path, with each `/` written as `:`. No IP
  addresses. A port has to be percent-encoded as `%3A`, and every segment is percent-decoded
  before use. — §2, `:12-22`
- **Resolution algorithm** (§3.2, `:33-43`):
  1. Strip `did:web:`.
  2. Split on `:`.
  3. Percent-decode each segment.
  4. **Only if there are no path segments**, append `/.well-known`.
  5. Append `/did.json`.
  6. Prefix `https://`.
  7. GET the URL.
  8. The document's `id` must equal the DID.
- Worked examples (§3.2 table, `:45-50`):
  - `did:web:w3c-ccg.github.io:user:alice` → `https://w3c-ccg.github.io/user/alice/did.json`.
    There's no `.well-known` when a path is present.
  - `did:web:example.com%3A3000` → `https://example.com:3000/.well-known/did.json`.
- HTTPS only, with no fallback to HTTP. The GET is the **only** source of the document. "the
  document is not derivable from the identifier". — `:52-53`
- **Update:** the controller replaces the document at its URL. Keys are added, rotated and
  removed this way, and no history is exposed. "the document currently served at the URL **is**
  the DID document." — §3.3, `:57-60`
- **Deactivate:** remove the document. After that, resolution fails. — §3.4, `:64-65`
- **Verifying a proof** (§4, `:69-76`): the verifier resolves the DID *when it verifies the
  proof*. It then dereferences `verificationMethod`, checks that the method is listed under the
  right relationship (`assertionMethod` for an issuer, `authentication` for a holder), and
  verifies against a `Multikey` / `publicKeyMultibase` Ed25519 key (`0xed01`).
- "A key that no longer appears in the document served at the DID's URL is not a key of the DID.
  A proof is valid only if it verifies against a verification method in the current document."
  — §4, `:78-79`
- Caching is allowed within the `Cache-Control` lifetime the host returns. — §4, `:81`
- Controllers are expected to rotate keys. Rotation takes effect for every verifier as soon as
  the new document is served. — §5, `:87-88`
- There's no self-certification. Unlike `did:key` and `did:peer`, the identifier carries no key
  material. — §5, `:89-90`
- `did:webvh` exists but "is not used on the platform". — §5, `:91-93`

## 2. Trust Registry contract (`reference/trust-registry.md`)

- It's run by the Governance team. It implements TRQP and is based on `affinidi-trust-registry-rs`.
  — `:3-5`
- The registry is the authority on which issuers are trusted to issue which credentials.
  "An issuer being onboarded, having a resolvable DID, or having signed a credential correctly
  does not make it trusted; a registry record does." — `:9-11`
- A record is keyed on the entity's DID. Its fields are `entity_id`, `authority_id` (=
  `did:web:governance.membership-platform.example`), `action` (`issue`), `resource` (e.g.
  `MembershipCredential`) and `status` (`active` / `suspended` / `withdrawn`). — `:13-22`
- The interface is `POST /authorization`. The request and response shapes are at `:26-48`.
  `authorized` is true only when the record's status is `active`. An unknown `entity_id` returns
  `200` with `authorized: false`, not an error. — `:50-51`
- `POST /recognition` is for authorities and isn't used by relying parties. — `:53-54`
- **Invariant** (`:58-62`):
  - A relying party must query the registry, at verification time, for the credential's `issuer`
    DID, action `issue` and the credential's type.
  - It must refuse the credential unless `authorized` is `true`.
  - Consumers must **not** keep their own list of trusted issuers. Records can be suspended or
    withdrawn without notice.
  - An answer may be cached for at most 300 s.
- DID document changes (rotated keys, moved endpoints) don't change the registry record. "The
  record follows the DID." — `:64-65`
- Export dated 2026-09-01: all four issuers are `active` for `issue` / `MembershipCredential`.
  — `:69-74`

  | entity_id | since |
  |---|---|
  | `did:web:members.harbourclub.example` | 2025-03-14 |
  | `did:web:issuer.cedarrowing.example` | 2025-05-02 |
  | `did:web:guild.northfield.example:chapters:north` | 2025-06-20 |
  | `did:web:badges.kestrel-league.example` | 2025-09-08 |

## 3. DID hosting (`reference/infra/did-hosting.md`)

- Issuers publish their `did:web` documents through the platform bucket
  `s3://issuer-did-documents-prod`, which has versioning on, behind CloudFront `E2T9QK4ZC1MX7B`.
  — `:3-9`
- The object key is `<host>/<path>`, "exactly the path part of the DID's HTTPS URL". — `:10`
  - `did:web:<host>` → `<host>/.well-known/did.json`. — `:11`
  - `did:web:<host>:<p1>:<p2>` → `<host>/<p1>/<p2>/did.json`. There's **no** `.well-known` when a
    path is present. — `:12`
- It's served with `Content-Type: application/did+json` and `Cache-Control: max-age=300`. — `:13-14`
- Only the issuer console writes objects, with one IAM role per issuer. — `:15`
- Adding, rotating or retiring a key, or changing an endpoint, writes a new object version and
  invalidates the CDN path. The old version stays in bucket history but "is no longer served".
  — `:17-20`
- `hosted-dids/` is a copy of the bucket's **current** objects. — `:22`

## 4. Hosted DID documents (`reference/infra/hosted-dids/`)

This is the current published state, per `did-hosting.md:22`. Every document uses `Multikey`, and
each has a single key listed under both `authentication` and `assertionMethod`.

| DID | Object path | Key id | `publicKeyMultibase` | LinkedDomains |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `did:web:members.harbourclub.example` | `members.harbourclub.example/.well-known/did.json` | `#key-1` | `z6MkjgN85p…vt6N` | `https://harbourclub.example/` |
| `did:web:issuer.cedarrowing.example` | `issuer.cedarrowing.example/.well-known/did.json` | `#key-2` | `z6MkvbwHpL…uRq9` | `https://cedarrowing.example/` |
| `did:web:guild.northfield.example:chapters:north` | `guild.northfield.example/chapters/north/did.json` (no `.well-known`) | `#signing` | `z6MkoBtQgt…MReJ7` | `https://guild.northfield.example/` |
| `did:web:badges.kestrel-league.example` | `badges.kestrel-league.example/.well-known/did.json` | `#key-2026` | `z6MksRrY1T…HZq1` | `https://kestrel-league.example/members/` |

Line references: each file's `verificationMethod` is at `:7-14`, and its `service` is at `:21-27`.

## 5. status-notifier deployment (`reference/infra/webhook-config.yaml`)

- This is a snapshot of `services/status-notifier/deploy.yaml`, owned by Platform Infrastructure,
  for production in eu-west-1. — `:1-8`
- **Trigger:** one invocation per status-change event (`batch_size: 1`,
  `starting_position: latest`). — `:10-14`
- **Timeout:** `timeout_seconds: 10` is a **hard** limit. "The runtime terminates the invocation
  when it is reached; work still in progress at that point is abandoned." — `:20-22`
- **No retries:** `maximum_retry_attempts: 0`, `maximum_event_age_seconds: 60`,
  `on_failure_destination: none`. — `:24-27`
- `reserved_concurrency: 20`. — `:23`
- **Network:** public egress through NAT, with `outbound_connect_timeout_ms: 2000`. — `:29-31`
- **`tenant-settings` table** (`:33-44`):
  - Partition key `tenant` (the issuer DID), sort key `setting_id`.
  - `query_page_size: 100`.
  - GSI `tenant-kind-index` (partition `tenant`, sort `kind`, projection all).
  - The service has read-only access.
- **Alarms:** `alarms: []`, i.e. none are configured. — `:51-53`

## 6. Reserved domains standard PI-STD-014 (`reference/infra/reserved-domains.md`)

- A reserved documentation or testing name must not appear as a live endpoint in any production
  config or code path. That includes webhooks, callbacks, health probes, synthetic monitoring,
  and "the targets of any check whose result is reported as the state of a platform service".
  — `:8-11`
- The reserved names are `example.com`, `example.net` and `example.org` (RFC 2606 §3). — `:15-22`
- These names resolve, and an IANA server may answer. Traffic to them leaves the platform, and "a
  response from one says nothing about the state of any platform service." — `:24-26`
- What to use instead:
  - For probes: an endpoint the platform operates, reached over the same path as the real
    traffic.
  - For tests: an in-process or loopback stub. — `:30-34`
- Enforcement is config linting of `deploy.yaml` files only. — `:38`
- Note: this doc lists only the three second-level names. It doesn't mention `.example` as a TLD.

## Open questions (the reference docs don't answer these)

- None of these documents explains the ticket's phrase "re-approved last month". The registry
  export (`trust-registry.md:69-74`) shows only the original `since` dates.
- None of them says when each issuer rotated its key. `did-hosting.md:19-20` says the history
  exists in bucket versioning, but we don't have a copy of it.
- It isn't stated which component production uses as the `DocumentTransport` (a real HTTPS
  client vs. a mirror). The only transports in the repo are `MirrorTransport` and
  `StaticTransport`.

I'm stretching the promise's wording slightly there; tell me if you read it differently.

5. **The health check measures the canary, not subscribers.** It's sent first, before any subscriber, and its result is independent of theirs. It points at a reserved domain in production, and at a stub that always says 200 in tests. **Breaks (C).**

## 3. What the health check actually checks

`canary_healthy()` returns one flag (`notifier.rs:130-132`). That flag is set only from the result of **the canary's own POST** for the latest change (`:143-145`). The canary is always posted to **first**, before the notifier has even read the tenant's subscriptions (`:141-147`). So it answers one question: did `https://example.com/webhooks/status` return 2xx? It says nothing about any customer's subscribers.
- **In tests,** `HermeticTransport` hard-wires that host to an instant 200 (`webhook.rs:84-87`).
- **In production,** the host is IANA's server. PI-STD-014 says a response from it "says nothing about the state of any platform service" (`reserved-domains.md:24-26`).

The last test above shows the check stays green in both ticket scenarios. With the large account, it's green while 3 of 3 subscribers are not told. With a hung endpoint, it's green while 2 of 2 healthy subscribers are not told. The timing sweep found the same: `canary_healthy=true` on every run, including 0 of 3 delivered.

## 4. Causes, and which confirmed promise each one breaks

The promises, as I'll refer to them:
- **(A)** Every subscribed relying party is told, whatever the size of the customer's account.
- **(B)** Every subscribed relying party is told, however any one relying party's endpoint behaves.
- **(C)** A green health check means callbacks are reaching customers.

1. **Every notification reads the customer's whole settings partition before sending anything** (`notifier.rs:158-169`). It pages through all of it at 50 ms per 100 settings, instead of using the `tenant-kind` index (`settings.rs:100-113`). At about 20,000 settings, the reading alone uses up the 10 s budget, so no subscriber is attempted. This is the ticket's customer: every revocation, every subscriber. **Breaks (A).**

2. **Deliveries go out one at a time, inside a single 10 s budget** (`notifier.rs:147-149`, `:152`). At 150 ms each, subscriber 67 onward never gets a callback. The budget matches the runtime's hard kill (`webhook-config.yaml:22`), so in production the runtime kills the work even if the code's own timeout didn't. **Breaks (A):** a large account also means many subscribers.

3. **There's no per-call timeout** (`notifier.rs:173`). The deployment only limits the connect (`webhook-config.yaml:31`, inference). One relying party that is slow or never answers holds the loop until the budget runs out, and every subscriber queued after it is dropped. **Breaks (B)** for all the other subscribers, which the tests show. It isn't the reported customer's cause as far as we know; it's a separate route to the same symptom, affecting any customer.

4. **Abandoned work leaves no trace, and nothing retries.** When the budget runs out, only an `eprintln!` is written. The subscribers that were never attempted get no failure event (`notifier.rs:152-154`); the sink test shows only the canary's event. There's no retry in code (`:172-181`) or in the deployment (`webhook-config.yaml:25-27`), and no alarms (`:53`). *Inference:* the log line probably never appears in production, since the runtime is killed at the same 10 s. This is why nobody noticed. It doesn't lose callbacks by itself, but it means a lost one is never recovered. **Breaks (A) and (B)** in the sense that "is told" never becomes true later. I'm stretching the promise's wording slightly there; tell me if you read it differently.

5. **The health check measures the canary, not subscribers.** It's sent first, before any subscriber, and its result is independent of theirs. It points at a reserved domain in production, and at a stub that always says 200 in tests. **Breaks (C).**

On current evidence, cause 1 is the most likely explanation for the reported customer: every revocation, all of that customer's subscribers, other customers fine. Causes 2 and 3 hit any customer that crosses the threshold, or that has one bad endpoint. Cause 5 is why the dashboard never showed any of it.
